title: Pretrees
author: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic)
description: Sets with a betweenness relation that behaves as in a tree. The first lesson gives the four axioms of a pretree, their consequences for four points, intervals, and the theorem that every finite pretree is a set of vertices of a finite tree with the betweenness of the tree, by an explicit construction from adjacent points and maximal cliques. It follows that linear sets have exactly two directions, that intervals are ordered, and that three points have at most one median. The second lesson treats dense, complete and median pretrees: a half-open interval of a dense pretree determines its open end; a complete dense pretree need not be median (an explicit example); in dense median pretrees an interval [x,y) inside [x,z] has y in [x,z]; and in complete dense median pretrees every cut of an interval is made at a point, so that intervals are ordered sets without gaps. The third lesson defines separable median pretrees, shows that a weakly dense set becomes strongly dense when medians are added, proves Cantor's theorem on countable dense orders, and concludes that in a complete separable median pretree every interval is ordered like the real interval [0,1]. The fourth lesson proves that a compact space with a countable dense subset and a complete dense median pretree structure whose sets H(x,y) are open is a dendrite, in which the intervals of the pretree are the only arcs. The fifth lesson introduces flows, the binary relations that describe a direction towards a place that need not be a point: the flow towards a point, the pretree obtained by adding one point for a flow, and the pretree formed by a pretree together with all its flows. The sixth lesson treats directed arcs: the flow of a directed arc, cofinal arcs, restriction to full subsets, suprema, and the theorem that a pretree is complete exactly when every directed arc has a supremum. The seventh lesson constructs the completion: the set of all flows of a pretree, with a betweenness read off from the points between flows, is a complete median pretree that contains the given pretree. The eighth lesson defines stars and their flows and proves that every flow on a nonempty pretree is of exactly one of three kinds: the flow towards a point, the flow of a star, or the flow of an endless directed arc. The ninth lesson determines the adjacent points of the completion: of two adjacent points exactly one is a point of the given pretree, and the neighbours of such a point correspond to the branches of the pretree at it. The tenth lesson treats discrete pretrees, those with finite intervals: a discrete median pretree is the vertex set of exactly one tree, every discrete pretree is a set of vertices of a tree whose further vertices are joined to at least three of its points, and the completion of a finite pretree is the vertex set of a finite tree. The eleventh lesson constructs quotients: for an equivalence relation whose classes are full, the set of classes is a pretree, intervals map onto intervals, and the quotient of a median or complete pretree is median or complete. The twelfth lesson treats the dense quotient: among the full relations with dense quotient there is a least one; it identifies two points exactly when no set of points ordered like the rational numbers lies between them, and it is reached from equality by repeatedly identifying points joined by finite intervals; the dense quotient of the completion is a complete dense median pretree. The thirteenth lesson gives the main example: a connected Hausdorff space is a pretree when a point lies between two others if it separates them; it treats separations at a point, branches, and coherent sets, and shows that every intersection of branches of a compact connected space is connected. The fourteenth lesson maps a pretree to the completion of a subset, each point going to the flow towards it, and shows for a compact connected Hausdorff space and a set of its cut points that every point of the completion is the image of a point of the space or adjacent to the image of a cut point. The fifteenth lesson constructs the dendrite quotient of a compact connected Hausdorff space: two points are identified unless a set of cut points ordered like the rational numbers separates them; the quotient is a continuum, the quotient map has connected fibres, and with a countable dense subset the quotient is a dendrite. A continuum with a countable dense subset in which any two points are separated by a third is a dendrite. Pretrees are the structure carried by the cut points of a continuum; they are used in OpenAI's proof (2026) of the Singer conjecture in dimension four outside the middle degree.
prerequisites: graphs, paths, cycles and connected graphs (definitions only)
for the fourth lesson: the course Continua, arcs and cut points (arcs, dendrites) and the Urysohn metrization theorem (core course Point-Set Topology)
for the twelfth lesson: ordinal numbers, transfinite recursion and Hartogs' lemma (core course Mathematical Logic, Set Theory, and Computability)
for the thirteenth lesson: connected, compact and Hausdorff spaces (core course Point-Set Topology)
the course proves every other fact it uses

checks.reading: Written on 11 Oct 2026 against Section 2 of Bowditch's memoir (author's version, library copy free/authors/bowditch/bhb-treelike.pdf, pages 10-14 read as page images). The embedding of finite pretrees in finite trees is proved by a construction different from the memoir's induction: the tree is built from the adjacency graph, with one new vertex for every maximal clique of at least three points. Each proof was re-read step by step; three slips were corrected (a wrong lemma citation, a missing clause, an inconsistent exercise). Lesson 2 was written against pages 15-16 of the memoir. Its Lemmas 2.8, 2.10 and 2.11 are false as stated: the lesson gives a counterexample (a tripod with a half-open segment next to the centre removed is complete and dense but not median) and proves the first two with the hypothesis 'median' added; findings ledger F-0011. Lesson 3 was written against page 16 of the memoir (Lemmas 2.12 and 2.13); the proof of Lemma 2.12 is written out with gates in a finite tree, and Cantor's theorem is proved. Lesson 4 was written against pages 17-18 of the memoir (Theorem 2.14, Lemmas 2.15-2.19) with the hypothesis 'median' stated; the countable base is proved from the sets H(p,q) directly, and every statement about medians is checked by gates in a finite tree. Lesson 5 was written against pages 23-24 of the memoir (flows, Lemmas 3.1-3.3); every case of the pretree axioms for the pretree with all flows is written out. Lesson 6 was written against pages 26-29 of the memoir (Lemmas 3.5-3.13). Cofinality is defined with agreement of the two orders on the common final segment, which the memoir leaves implicit; the restriction lemma (3.11) is proved through the pretree with one added point, because the memoir's reduction does not cover the case where a point of the pair lies on the arc; the completeness criterion (3.13), stated there without proof, is proved. Lesson 7 was written against pages 29-32 of the memoir (Lemmas 3.14-3.18, Theorem 3.19); every step of the three parts of the proof (pretree axioms, medians, completeness) was re-derived, and Lemma 3.16 is obtained directly from the flow of a directed arc. Lesson 8 was written against pages 33-36 of the memoir (Lemmas 3.20-3.24, Proposition 3.25); every step was re-derived. The classification is stated with the type of a flow, so that the three kinds are shown to exclude each other and the star is shown to be determined by its flow; the set N(y) is taken with x ranging over the whole pretree, as the memoir's use of it requires. Lesson 9 was written against pages 36-38 of the memoir (Lemmas 3.26-3.29); every step was re-derived. The set L(a) is defined without the flow towards a, which the memoir's definition includes although its Lemma 3.26 excludes it; Lemma 3.29 is proved by an explicit bijection between the branches at a and L(a), in place of the memoir's case distinction. Lesson 10 was written against pages 39-40 of the memoir (Lemma 3.34, Proposition 3.35), which gives both statements without proof; the lesson proves the first directly (connectedness from finite intervals, no cycle from medians) and the second by the maximal-clique construction of the first lesson. The memoir's remark that the completion of a discrete pretree is discrete and has no flows of an endless arc is false; the lesson gives the integers as an example (ledger F-0015). Lesson 11 was written against pages 41-42 of the memoir (Lemmas 4.1, 4.2); every step was re-derived. The proof that a quotient of a complete pretree is complete is organised around the statement that the quotient map sends intervals onto intervals (Proposition 3.1 of the lesson), which also gives the statements on full sets and on quotients of quotients; the memoir's axiom (T3) for the quotient has a misprint (W different from Z for W different from Y). Lesson 12 was written against pages 42-45 of the memoir (Lemmas 4.3-4.5); every step was re-derived. The stabilisation of the transfinite process is proved with Hartogs' lemma (core course C80, Open Logic Project). In Lemma 4.5 the memoir uses that a point of T lies between any two distinct points of the completion, which fails for adjacent points; the lesson takes the point of T between two further points of the rational subset (Proposition 6.2). Lesson 13 was written against pages 45-48 of the memoir (Lemmas 5.1-5.9); every step was re-derived. Lemma 5.4 is stated in the memoir with 'U a connected component of the complement of a'; its proof and its uses need 'one side of a separation at a', and the lesson states it so (a branch with its boundary point removed need not be connected). Lemma 5.8 is proved without Zorn's lemma, through intersections of families closed under finite intersections. Lesson 14 was written against pages 48-49 of the memoir (Lemmas 5.10-5.13, Proposition 5.14); every step was re-derived. Lemma 5.10 uses that a point of T between x and y goes to a point between the images, which the lesson proves (Lemma 1.2(1)); Lemma 5.12 is proved without the embedding in a finite tree; the memoir's Proposition 5.14 is printed with the set R_M(p) 'empty' where 'not empty' is meant. Lesson 15 was written against pages 49-52 of the memoir (Lemmas 5.15-5.21, Proposition 5.22, Theorem 5.23); every step was re-derived. Theorem 5.23 rests on the memoir's Theorem 2.14, which the course proves with the hypothesis 'median' (lesson 4); the dense quotient of the completion is median, so the theorem holds. Proved in addition: the description of the fibres by rational sets of cut points (stated in the memoir as a remark), the note before Lemma 5.18 (a point of T separates), the lemma on maps with connected fibres, and that the pretree of the quotient is the pretree of its topology.

open_obligations: Not in the course: the memoir's remarks that the completion stays a complete median pretree after removing the flows of types (0,2) and (1,1), and its Lemmas 3.30-3.33 on complete embeddings and saturated pretrees.
Not in the course: group actions on these structures (Bowditch, Section 6); they belong to the course on convergence groups.
free_sources: B. H. Bowditch, Treelike structures arising from continua and convergence groups (author's version of Mem. Amer. Math. Soc. 662, 1999), Section 2
